You are a skeptical source-verifier. For EACH finding in the JSON below: use WebSearch/WebFetch (load via ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch" if needed) to confirm the named source exists and is accurately described. Mark exists=false for anything unconfirmable; corrections for anything misdescribed. Be strict.

FINDINGS JSON:
[{"name":"RACI responsibility-assignment matrix (RAM)","tradition":"Project management (PMI / systems-era PM literature)","source_type":"standard","citation":"PMI, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide), 6th ed., 2017 — Plan Resource Management (§9.1) data-representation tools and glossary: RAM = \"a grid that shows the project resources assigned to each work package\"; RACI chart = \"a common type of RAM that uses responsible, accountable, consult, and inform statuses to define the involvement of stakeholders in project activities\" (definitions confirmed via PMI-affiliated PMP literature quoting the Guide; RAM treatment sits at p. 262 in the 5th ed.). Ancestry: the Linear Responsibility Chart in Cleland & King, Systems Analysis and Project Management, McGraw-Hill, 1968 (see also PMI Library, \"Early Literature of Modern Project Management\", pmi.org/learning/library/early-literature-modern-project-management-3542). The R-A-C-I lettering itself has no documented single originator — the Wikipedia RAM article and PMI-adjacent literature carry no dated origin; folklore attributions (GE, 1950s) are unverified and should not be cited.","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Responsibility_assignment_matrix","what_it_defines":"A two-dimensional matrix crossing work items (rows: tasks, work packages, or deliverables) with roles (columns), each cell holding one involvement status: Responsible (does the work), Accountable (the one ultimately answerable for correct completion), Consulted (two-way input sought before/while), Informed (one-way notification after). The one-A rule — exactly one Accountable per row — is the form's load-bearing constraint; evidence status: the PMBOK glossary defines only the four statuses, while the one-A rule is stated as hard doctrine throughout PMI-affiliated exam/practitioner literature and is echoed at decision granularity by Bain's single-Decider rule (RAPID). Recurrent documented failure modes from practitioner criticism: (a) multiple As on one row dissolve accountability; (b) R/A conflation — the doer assumes they also judge sufficiency, removing oversight; (c) assigning R/A to a team rather than a named role/individual, so no one is individually answerable; (d) Consulted-list bloat slowing work; (e) shelfware — the chart is drafted once, never consulted, producing an illusion of clarity (e.g., tallyfy.com/raci-matrix and similar critiques; secondary sources, cited as criticism-in-circulation, not authority).","form_elements":["Rows: deliverables / work packages / tasks (the unit of assignment is the work item, not the role)","Columns: roles (positions, not persons)","Cell vocabulary: R / A / C / I with defined semantics (R = completes the work; A = solely answerable for correct completion; C = two-way consultation; I = one-way notification)","One-A-per-row rule: exactly one Accountable for each deliverable","Audit rules implied by the form: no empty rows, no row with zero or multiple As, flag rows with many Cs, every R/A a named role"],"fit_notes":"The system already enforces the one-A analog: report §2.2 adopts RUP's one-responsible-role-per-artifact rule, which is exactly a standing A column over artifact kinds. What RACI adds that the RUP rule lacks is the C/I dimension — precisely what the pending PO-vs-Architect RACI investigation needs: rows = artifact kinds and decision points (brief, PDR, scenario set, dispatch, clarify response, reconciliation), columns = lead-po, lead-architect, router, BC; the A column must reproduce the existing artifact→role bindings (a consistency check, not a new decision), while C and I capture what is currently only implicit in clarify-routing and Monitor-event rules (who is Consulted on a scope clarify, who is Informed of a work_done). Failure modes map directly: multiple-A = the ambiguous-clarify-routing problem the router rules already wrestle with; shelfware risk is structurally low here because definitions compile into agent context rather than living in a drawer — but only if the matrix is derived into role frontmatter/primers, not kept as a standalone page. Format note: the matrix is an assignment overlay across role definitions, not a role-definition container — it complements, not replaces, the §2.2 subagent-file form.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"RASCI and the RACI letter-set variant family","tradition":"Project management (practitioner extensions)","source_type":"practice","citation":"Variant inventory as carried on the Wikipedia RAM article (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Responsibility_assignment_matrix): RASCI/RACIS/RASIC/RASI (adds S = Support), RACIQ (Q = Quality review), RACIO/CAIRO (O = Omitted / out-of-the-loop), RACI-VS(L) (V = Verifier, S = Signatory), PARIS (Participant / Accountable / Review required / Input required / Sign-off required), RACI+F (Facilitation). No variant has a single authoritative standard; all are practitioner extensions of the PMBOK-carried base form.","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Responsibility_assignment_matrix","what_it_defines":"Letter-set extensions to the base RACI cell vocabulary, each adding a distinguished involvement status while preserving the matrix form and (in every variant) the one-A rule. The most adopted is RASCI: S = Support, a role that assists the Responsible in doing the work without owning it — splitting RACI's overloaded R into doer vs helper. RACI-VS is notable for adding V = Verifier (checks the deliverable against acceptance criteria) and S = Signatory (approves the verified result), pulling verification into the assignment matrix itself. CAIRO's O explicitly marks roles deliberately excluded from a work item.","form_elements":["Same matrix skeleton as RACI (work-item rows x role columns, one A per row)","S (Support): assists the Responsible without owning completion — doer/helper split","V (Verifier): checks the deliverable against defined acceptance criteria; distinct from both R and A","S (Signatory): formally approves after verification","O (Omitted/out-of-the-loop): explicit exclusion marker","Q (Quality review): a named quality-check involvement"],"fit_notes":"Mostly context: the variant explosion is itself evidence of the base form's expressive gap, and the report should describe rather than adopt the zoo. Two letters have real resonance here. S (Support) matches the dispatched-subagent-assists pattern (a lead-architect dispatch supporting a router-owned reconciliation). V (Verifier) is the interesting one for a system whose thesis is construction-definitions-precede-checks: a Verifier column names, per artifact kind, the role that runs the derived checks (LLM judge, reviewer role), keeping judge separate from generator — which §3's Goodharting mitigations already require. If the PO-vs-Architect matrix is built, RASCI-with-V (i.e., R/A/S/C/I plus a Verifier column) is a defensible shop dialect, provided each added letter carries a Deming-style operational definition rather than a vibe.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"Decision-rights matrices: RAPID (Bain) and DACI (Intuit/Atlassian)","tradition":"Management consulting / product-org practice","source_type":"framework","citation":"RAPID: Rogers, P. & Blenko, M., \"Who Has the D?: How Clear Decision Roles Enhance Organizational Performance\", Harvard Business Review 84(1), January 2006 (hbr.org/2006/01/who-has-the-d-how-clear-decision-roles-enhance-organizational-performance; also bain.com/insights/who-has-the-d/) — Recommend / Agree / Perform / Input / Decide, exactly one Decider; identifies four recurring decision-bottleneck loci (global vs local, center vs business unit, function vs function, inside vs outside partners). DACI: Atlassian Team Playbook, \"DACI: A Decision-Making Framework\" (atlassian.com/team-playbook/plays/daci) — Driver / Approver / Contributors / Informed, one Approver; origin commonly attributed to Intuit in the 1980s (secondary attribution only, not primary-verified).","url":"https://hbr.org/2006/01/who-has-the-d-how-clear-decision-roles-enhance-organizational-performance","what_it_defines":"The decision-rights fork of the responsibility matrix: the unit of assignment is a DECISION, not a task or deliverable. RAPID assigns five roles per decision — Recommend (builds the proposal), Agree (must consent, a constrained veto), Input (consulted, voice not vote), Decide (the single D, commits the organization), Perform (executes once decided) — and was explicitly motivated by the failure mode RACI does not fix: task matrices leave decision authority ambiguous. DACI's contribution is splitting the two roles organizations systematically merge: the Driver (moves the decision process to a conclusion by an agreed date) vs the Approver (holds final authority). Both preserve the exactly-one-decider invariant.","form_elements":["Unit of assignment: a named decision (not a task/deliverable)","Exactly one Decide/Approver per decision (the one-A rule at decision granularity)","Recommend/Driver as a distinct process-ownership role separate from authority","Agree: consent-required role with bounded veto (RAPID)","Input/Contributors: voice-not-vote consultation","Perform: execution role bound after the decision","Named bottleneck taxonomy for locating which decisions need explicit role assignment (RAPID)"],"fit_notes":"Directly relevant to the PO-vs-Architect investigation, because that question is partly decision-rights, not task assignment: who DECIDES scope vocabulary vs message-type selection vs decomposition is cleaner in RAPID terms than in RACI terms (the shop's discriminator rules are, in effect, an implicit D-assignment: PO holds the D on scope/vocabulary, Architect on vehicle/decomposition, the product authority on ratification). The Driver/Approver split maps to router-vs-authority: the router drives classification and dispatch to conclusion but never holds product authority — DACI names that separation precisely. Recommend describing both in §1.2's successor section and borrowing only the vocabulary: per-decision single-D assignments folded into role accountabilities, not a standalone RAPID chart. The Intuit origin claim for DACI must stay marked as unverified attribution if cited.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"Holacracy role format and governance amendment process","tradition":"Self-management / sociocracy lineage","source_type":"framework","citation":"Holacracy Constitution v5.0, HolacracyOne (holacracy.org/constitution/5-0/; source text at github.com/holacracyone/Holacracy-Constitution, CC BY-SA 4.0): §1.1 role definition (name + Purpose + Domains + Accountabilities), §1.2/§1.4.1 role assignment and Role Lead, Article 5 governance process — §5.3.1 valid-proposal criteria (tension + concrete example + how the proposal reduces it), §5.3.2–5.3.3 objection-testing criteria, §5.4.5 integrative decision-making sequence. Book form: Robertson, B., Holacracy: The New Management System for a Rapidly Changing World, Henry Holt, 2015. Failure exemplar: Doyle, A., \"Management and Organization at Medium\", Medium blog, March 2016 (blog.medium.com/management-and-organization-at-medium-2228cc9d93e9) — Medium's exit after several years: coordination tax at scale, and \"the act of codifying responsibilities in explicit detail hindered a proactive attitude and sense of communal ownership.\"","url":"https://www.holacracy.org/constitution/5-0/","what_it_defines":"A constitutionalized role anatomy with strict role/person separation. A Role is a descriptive name plus three optional parts (§1.1): Purpose — \"a capacity, potential, or goal that the Role will pursue or express\"; Domains — \"assets, processes, or other things the Role may exclusively control and regulate as its property\"; Accountabilities — \"ongoing activities the Role will manage and enact\", by convention phrased as gerunds (\"Implementing…\", \"Designing…\"), a lintable authoring rule. People are not roles: a person filling a role is its Role Lead; Circle Leads assign roles (§1.4.1); one person may fill many roles and one role many people. Role definitions can be changed ONLY through the Governance Process (Article 5): a proposal must be grounded in a concrete Tension the proposer's role experienced (§5.3.1); it is processed through integrative decision-making (present → clarifying questions → reaction round → amend → objection round → integration, §5.4.5); objections must pass defined validity tests (§5.3.2) or the proposal stands. Governance outputs are recorded role amendments — an append/amend audit trail of the role set.","form_elements":["Role = descriptive name + Purpose + Domains + Accountabilities (each part optional, all three typed)","Purpose: one-line pursued capacity/goal (why the role exists)","Domains: exclusive-control grants — property the role alone may regulate","Accountabilities: ongoing-activity list, gerund-phrased (verb-ing), not task scripts","Role/person separation: Role Lead assignment distinct from role definition; many-to-many","Amendment protocol: tension-grounded proposal + integrative decision-making + objection-validity tests; definition changes only via governance, recorded","Policies: named grants/constraints of authority attachable to domains"],"fit_notes":"The strongest external match found for this system's role layer. (a) Role/person separation maps exactly to definition-vs-instance: the .claude/agents file is the role, a dispatched subagent run is a Role Lead energizing it. (b) Domains are the missing formal name for the shop's exclusive bindings — RUP's one-responsible-role-per-artifact rule (§2.2) is precisely a Domain grant (\"the PO exclusively controls features/ scenarios\"), and phrasing artifact bindings as Domains would make the one-A property a structural feature of the role definition rather than a matrix-side rule. (c) Gerund accountability lists are near-isomorphic to the Scrum-style 4–8 accountability bullets §2.2 already recommends; Holacracy adds the enforceable phrasing convention. (d) The governance amendment protocol is an established, citable form for what the report elsewhere requires ad hoc — TOGAF's \"stable but amendable under a change process\" (§2.4) and the gated canonical-template promotion (§2.7): tension-grounded proposals with objection tests are a concrete protocol for amending role definitions under change control. Cautions: adopt the anatomy and amendment discipline, not the machinery (circles, elected facilitators, tactical meetings — heavy, human-meeting-shaped); and Medium's documented exit reason — exhaustive codification taxing proactivity — is a live risk for a system that compiles role text into agent context, arguing for Holacracy's own minimalism (all three role parts optional) plus the existing 200-line primer budget.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"Team Topologies team types and interaction modes","tradition":"Software organization design","source_type":"book","citation":"Skelton, M. & Pais, M., Team Topologies: Organizing Business and Technology Teams for Fast Flow, IT Revolution Press, 2019; concept definitions maintained at teamtopologies.com/key-concepts (wording verified): four team types — stream-aligned, enabling, complicated-subsystem, platform — and three interaction modes — collaboration (\"working together for a defined period of time to discover new things\"), X-as-a-Service (\"one team provides and one team consumes something 'as a Service'\"), facilitating (\"one team helps and mentors another team\").","url":"https://teamtopologies.com/key-concepts","what_it_defines":"Role-adjacent, not a role-definition format: it types TEAMS (not persons) into four kinds by their relationship to the flow of work, and — the transferable part — types the RELATIONSHIP between any two teams into exactly three interaction modes, each with defined semantics and an expected evolution (collaboration is deliberately time-bounded and should decay into X-as-a-Service as interfaces stabilize). The claim is that naming the interaction mode is itself an organizational design act: ambiguous inter-team relationships are a primary source of friction, and the three-mode vocabulary makes the intended relationship explicit and reviewable.","form_elements":["Four team types: stream-aligned (owns a flow of change), enabling (helps stream-aligned teams overcome obstacles, detects missing capabilities), complicated-subsystem (deep-specialism component), platform (internal product accelerating stream-aligned teams)","Three interaction modes: collaboration (time-bounded joint discovery), X-as-a-Service (provider/consumer over a stable interface, minimal coordination), facilitating (one team mentors another)","Evolution rule: interaction modes are expected to shift over time (collaboration → X-as-a-Service) and the shift is a designed decision","Per-relationship declaration: each pair of teams names its current intended mode"],"fit_notes":"Included because it is the only verified established form that types role-to-role INTERACTION, a dimension absent from every format in the current §1.2 survey and from RACI (which types involvement in a deliverable, not the standing relationship between two roles). The mapping to this system is clean: lead-shop↔BC is X-as-a-Service by construction (the shop-msg contract, ADR-018's no-BC-source rule — the interface IS the service boundary); a clarify exchange is bounded collaboration; lead-architect answering BC clarifies verges on facilitating. Adoption should be limited to the interaction-mode triad as declared vocabulary — e.g., a role definition or primer names its intended mode per counterpart, making \"the router does not collaborate with BCs, it consumes them as a service\" a stated, checkable line rather than folklore. The four team types themselves are org-design for human teams and should stay descriptive context only.","adopt_potential":"context-only"}]

- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- bring-up-bc: Launch an already-scaffolded Bounded Context as a running, online container and verify it reaches the online state
- company-research: Build a cited, bounded intelligence brief on a competitor, peer product, or alternative framework — strategy, product philosophy, recent moves — to ground a brief/PDR in external reality instead of intuition. Use for the consumer-product competitive/market input to problem discovery, or to study a competing framework.
- create-bc: Create a new Bounded Context from scratch — scaffold, remote, manifest registration, and brokered launch — as the lead shop
- derisk-measurement-advisor: Scan a shaping candidate for risk across 10 dimensions — 4 internal (Desirability, Usability, Feasibility, Viability) and 6 external (PESTEL) — and triage each into act-now or track, so the candidate's rabbit-holes and risks name what to test before committing. Reach for it when a bet feels roadmap-ready and you want a structured "what could go wrong, internally and externally?"
- discovery-dialogue: Run the open, interactive discovery conversation that turns a directional or ambiguous prompt into a written, grounded intent record
- discovery-interview-prep: Design a customer discovery interview plan — research goal, target segment, access constraints, and a bias-resistant question set — so a discovery-dialogue turn produces real learning instead of confirmation. Use when the intent record rests on an assumed job that needs to be heard from a real user.
- discovery-process: The end-to-end discovery arc — frame, plan, research, synthesize, validate, decide — used to sequence a multi-turn discovery-dialogue and know which technique skill comes next. Use when a discovery is large enough to need staging rather than a single lens.
- eol-message: Empathetic end-of-life announcement for a retiring product or capability — acknowledges disruption, explains the change as progress, and gives a concrete migration path. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session, and specifically when a brief flips to status:retired.
- incoming-request-advisor: Decode an incoming request before responding — separate the literal ask from the job-behind-it, read the sender's power and stake, and surface hidden assumptions — so a request is classified by its real outcome, not its surface wording. Use at PM-mode entry, at the router's classification boundary, to decide whether a request needs a discovery-dialogue at all.
- jobs-to-be-done: Uncover the stable job a user is hiring the product to do — functional, social, emotional — plus their pains and gains, so intent anchors on a validated job instead of a feature request. Use during the discovery-dialogue when a request smells solution-shaped ("add X").
- opportunity-solution-tree: Move from a target outcome down through opportunities (problems) to candidate solutions to a chosen bet, so shaping commits the candidate to the right problem before it converges on a sketch. Reach for it when a request arrives outcome-shaped or solution-shaped and you need to keep "what are we moving?" upstream of "what do we build?"
- option-tradeoff: Frame two or more shaped options against each other, surface the tradeoffs, and run the deciding conversation with the product authority
- pol-probe: Design a Proof-of-Life probe — a lightweight, disposable experiment that tests one falsifiable hypothesis before expensive work — and land it in the candidate's evidence/experiments line. Reach for it when a shape rests on an assumption cheap enough to test in hours or days and honest enough to kill the bet if it fails.
- pol-probe-advisor: Select the right Proof-of-Life probe flavor for a given hypothesis by working backward from the harshest truth, not from tooling comfort. Reach for it inside shaping when you know an assumption needs testing but aren't sure whether it's a feasibility check, a task test, a narrative, a simulation, or a vibe-coded probe.
- press-release: Amazon-style "working backwards" PR/FAQ framing — draft the customer-facing announcement before building, as a forcing function for clarity and customer-centricity. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session to test whether a direction is genuinely compelling from the outside.
- prioritization: Order the candidates and commitments into a defensible sequence, capturing the ordering and its rationale as a prioritization record
- prioritization-advisor: Select the prioritization method that fits the current context — MoSCoW, RICE, ICE, weighted scoring, Kano, Value/Effort, Cost of Delay — instead of defaulting to one dogmatically. Reach for it inside a prioritization session before scoring anything, to pick the right lens for the stage, data, and decision at hand.
- problem-framing-canvas: Reframe a messy or solution-shaped request into a clear, bias-checked problem statement and a "How Might We" question before committing intent. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when you suspect you're about to solve the wrong problem.
- problem-space-mapping: Continuously maintain the map of the product's problem space so every candidate and intent has a place to hang, producing problem-space map revisions
- problem-statement: Turn a request or a raw job into a crisp, user-centered problem statement using the "I am / trying to / but / because / which makes me feel" frame, so intent names a person and a barrier, not a solution. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to fix the problem before any solutioning.
- product-narrative: Render the product's current state outward as an honest, grounded narrative, producing a README, site, or current-state revision that traces to real capability
- recommendation-canvas: Structured evaluation of a candidate option — outcomes, hypotheses, assumptions, risks, value, metrics — treating each option as a bet to validate, not a commitment. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to turn a raw option list into a defensible pick with rationale.
- reconcile-and-close: Reconcile a completed BC dispatch by consuming its work_done outbox row and closing the corresponding bead as one atomic reconcile-and-close action via the reconcile-and-close executable wrapper
- shaping: Take a validated intent and drive a single candidate to shaped — bounded, de-risked, and ready for a commitment decision
- stakeholder-engagement-advisor: Plan engagement for one specific stakeholder — diagnose their profile and power/impact position, then tailor message, medium, cadence, and a named next action, planning both sides of the relationship. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when the intent hinges on a critical or resistant stakeholder whose input you must actually secure.
- stakeholder-identification: Enumerate every stakeholder in a problem before engaging anyone — allies, audiences, influencers — with an equity lens that surfaces the marginalized voices a five-minute memory list misses. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to be sure the intent isn't framed for only the loudest party.
- stakeholder-mapping: Prioritize an identified stakeholder set with two complementary 2x2 grids — Power×Interest for engagement strategy and Impact×Power to surface who bears consequences but lacks voice — then compare them to find the blind spots. Use inside the discovery-dialogue after identification to decide whose voice the intent must elevate.
- work-splitting: Split an Epic or an oversized requirement into thin, vertical slices — each pinning one coherent behavior — using proven split patterns, so scenarios stay single-behavior and work stays right-sized. Use when decomposing an Epic into scenarios, when a scenario carries multiple When/Then, or when an assigned unit is too big to build and review cleanly.
- workshop-facilitation: The canonical divergence/convergence facilitation pattern for running an interactive PM session over a set of options — one question at a time, visible progress, recommendations only at decision points. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to structure how the dialogue is conducted.
- write-adr: Use when the author is authoring or creating a adr artifact — a generated guide that drives the adr to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the adr kind.
- write-brief: Use when the author is authoring or creating a brief artifact — a generated guide that drives the brief to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the brief kind.
- write-candidate: Use when the author is authoring or creating a candidate artifact — a generated guide that drives the candidate to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the candidate kind.
- write-current-state: Use when the author is authoring or creating a current-state artifact — a generated guide that drives the current-state to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the current-state kind.
- write-intent-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a intent-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the intent-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the intent-record kind.
- write-pdr: Use when the author is authoring or creating a pdr artifact — a generated guide that drives the pdr to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the pdr kind.
- write-prioritization-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a prioritization-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the prioritization-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the prioritization-record kind.
- write-session-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a session-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the session-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the session-record kind.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation

# DACI Decision-Making Framework Analysis

Yes, this page describes the DACI decision-making framework. The acronym stands for:

- **D = Driver**: "The person responsible for corralling stakeholders, collating all the necessary information, determining the scope of the decision, and getting a decision made by the agreed date."

- **A = Approver**: "The one person (yes: one!) who makes the decision."

- **C = Contributors**: "People who have subject-area knowledge and can make recommendations – i.e., they have a voice, but not a vote."

- **I = Informed**: "People whose work may be affected by the decision, and should be informed once it's been made – i.e., no vote, no voice."

## Origin Note

The page does **not** mention an origin at Intuit in the 1980s. There is a reference to a McKinsey & Company survey about DACI effectiveness, but no historical attribution to Intuit or a specific founding date is provided in this content.

# Holacracy Constitution v5.0 Analysis

**Is this version 5.0?** Yes, this is the Holacracy Constitution Version 5.0.

**Section 1.1 Role Definition:** Yes, section 1.1 defines a Role as consisting of a descriptive name and one or more of:

- **Purpose:** "a capacity, potential, or goal that the Role will pursue or express"
- **Domains:** "assets, processes, or other things the Role may exclusively control and regulate as its property"
- **Accountabilities:** "ongoing activities the Role will manage and enact in service of other Roles or to support its Purpose"

**Article 5 - Governance Process:** Yes, Article 5 describes the Governance Process. Key section numbers:

- **Valid Proposals (Tension-grounded):** Section 5.3.1 requires proposers to describe a Tension, provide an example, and explain how the proposal addresses it
- **Objection Testing:** Section 5.3.3 outlines testing criteria for valid objections
- **Integrative Decision-Making:** Section 5.4.5 details the step-by-step process including proposal presentation, clarifying questions, reactions, objection rounds, and integration

# Team Topologies: Four Team Types and Three Interaction Modes

Yes, this page clearly defines both concepts.

## Four Team Types

The page lists all four:
- **Stream-aligned team**: "aligned to a flow of work from (usually) a segment of the business domain"
- **Enabling team**: "helps a Stream-aligned team to overcome obstacles"
- **Complicated Subsystem team**: "where significant mathematics/calculation/technical expertise is needed"
- **Platform team**: "a grouping of other team types that provide a compelling internal product"

## Three Interaction Modes

The exact definitions provided are:

1. **Collaboration**: "working together for a defined period of time to discover new things (APIs, practices, technologies, etc.)"

2. **X-as-a-Service**: "one team provides and one team consumes something 'as a Service'"

3. **Facilitation**: "one team helps and mentors another team"

These definitions match precisely what you referenced, confirming the page contains the complete framework you inquired about.

The DACI Decision-Making Framework was developed by software company Intuit in the 1980s. The framework was created to address decision paralysis, which often arises when a team lacks ownership, leading to confusion about who makes the final call.

## Framework Details

DACI stands for driver, approver, contributor, and informed. The DACI framework originated as a variant of the RACI responsibility assignment matrix.

Since it was first used at Intuit 40 years ago, the DACI framework has since been adopted and adapted by many other companies. DACI was popularized at scale by Atlassian through its Team Playbook.

# RACI Matrix Critique: Main Failure Modes

Yes, this is fundamentally a critique of RACI matrices in practice. Here are the key criticisms:

## Core Failure Modes

**Static documentation problem**: The article's central thesis is that RACI matrices "fight human biology." People forget 90% of what they learn within seven days, rendering static charts obsolete within months.

**Shelfware accumulation**: Organizations create matrices, laminate them, hang them on walls, then abandon them. As the author notes, "most become expensive wall decorations" that gather dust by month three or six.

**Incompatibility with dynamic work**: The framework assumes stable roles and predictable processes, but "projects pivot, priorities shift, and key people leave the company," making documented assignments immediately inaccurate.

**Enforcement gaps**: The article highlights that "you can't force people to check a spreadsheet before every decision." Documentation lacks inherent enforcement mechanisms.

**Complexity defeats purpose**: Elaborate matrices become counterproductive. "The most elaborate RACI charts become expensive wall decorations; focus only on decisions that cause delays."

**Multiple accountability confusion**: The TechCorp case study illustrates how having three people marked "Accountable" creates confusion rather than clarity, with approval processes taking five days minimum.

**Political ambiguity as feature**: Some organizations unconsciously preserve RACI confusion because "ambiguity provides cover" and lets everyone claim credit.

The proposed alternative: embed responsibilities into automated workflows instead of static documents.
